name: Radio codes one bit apart
brief:
Each handset on a trading floor sends a 30-bit radio code, listed in `codes`. Two handsets interfere when their codes differ in exactly one bit. Several handsets may share a code; two with the same code differ in no bit, so they do not interfere.

Write `one_bit_pairs(codes)`, which returns the number of pairs of handsets, by position in the list, that interfere.

Example. For `codes = [5, 4, 7, 5, 1]`, each of the two handsets on 5 interferes with 4, 7 and 1, since 5 differs from them only in the bits worth 1, 2 and 4. No other pair differs in one bit, so the answer is 6.
constraints: $O(30\,n)$ time is the target. Comparing every pair is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Count how many handsets carry each code. For each code, flip each of its 30 bits in turn and look the result up in the counts. Count each pair of codes from its smaller end only.

examples.note: Both handsets on 5 pair with 4, 7 and 1, which makes 6 pairs.
Equal codes differ in no bit, so nothing interferes.

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. Comparing every pair is the obvious method and is $O(n^2)$; flipping each of the 30 bits of every distinct code and looking the result up is the target.
notes: Two codes differ in exactly one bit when one is the other with a single bit flipped, so 30 look-ups find every partner.
Counting a pair only from its smaller code stops it being counted twice, and equal codes are never partners.
There are at most $n$ distinct codes and 30 flips each, so the work is $O(30\,n)$.

planted.slip: Counting distinct codes only loses the extra pairs that each repeated code makes.
Looking up partners from both ends counts every pair twice.
Flipping only the bits up to the code's highest set bit never finds a partner with a higher bit set.
Comparing every pair is right but $O(n^2)$, far too slow for 100,000 codes.
